meta.title: Nephrology Literature Update
meta.query: Clinical nephrology — RCTs, systematic reviews & meta-analyses (humans, English)
meta.source: PubMed (NLM) abstracts; summaries and appraisals generated automatically from those abstracts. Each entry links to its PubMed record and DOI.
meta.note: Summaries and PICO are machine analyses of the source abstracts; criteria marked “not specified” were not stated. Read the source before acting clinically.
meta.appraisal_source: Automated critical appraisal (clinical bottom-line, relevance, caveat).

articles.title: Effects of intradialytic nutrition on dialysis adequacy and fatigue in hemodialysis patients: a randomized crossover study.
articles.summary: A randomized, two-period, two-sequence, self-controlled crossover trial in 36 maintenance hemodialysis patients in Türkiye (32 completed) comparing standardized intradialytic nutrition to no food intake. No significant differences were found in dialysis adequacy (URR, spKt/V) or fatigue scores (Piper Fatigue Scale). Intradialytic nutrition was associated with greater reductions in systolic and diastolic blood pressure, especially during the second hour.

pico.population: Maintenance hemodialysis patients in two outpatient centers in Türkiye (n=36 randomized, 32 completed)
pico.intervention: Standardized intradialytic nutrition during one period
pico.outcome: Dialysis adequacy (urea reduction ratio and single-pool Kt/V), fatigue severity (Piper Fatigue Scale), intradialytic blood pressure, and adverse events

inclusion: Maintenance hemodialysis patients from two outpatient hemodialysis centers in Türkiye

appraisal.bottom_line: Intradialytic nutrition did not significantly alter dialysis adequacy or fatigue scores compared to fasting, but it was associated with greater reductions in systolic and diastolic blood pressure, particularly during the second hour of dialysis.
appraisal.relevance: Nephrologists managing hemodialysis patients must balance nutritional support with hemodynamic stability, as intradialytic feeding may exacerbate intradialytic hypotension.
appraisal.caveat: The study has a very small sample size (36 randomized, 32 completed) and a short duration (crossover design, exact period lengths not specified), limiting its power to detect small differences in fatigue or adequacy, and it does not report long-term nutritional or cardiovascular outcomes.

articles.authors: Xiao Z, Fu C, Li W
articles.title: Effect of intradialytic exercise on cardiovascular structural and functional parameters in maintenance haemodialysis: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.summary: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 14 RCTs (934 participants) evaluating the impact of intradialytic exercise (IDE) versus usual care or non-exercise controls. IDE significantly increased left ventricular end-diastolic volume (MD 14.15 mL, 95% CI 2.06 to 26.24; p=0.022), improved left ventricular ejection fraction (MD 2.21%, 95% CI 0.28 to 4.15; p=0.025), reduced pulse wave velocity (MD -1.36 m/s, 95% CI -2.58 to -0.13; p=0.031), increased peak oxygen uptake (MD 2.76 mL/kg/min, 95% CI 0.08 to 5.43; p=0.044), and reduced diastolic blood pressure (MD -4.54 mmHg, 95% CI -7.57 to -1.51; p=0.003). No significant differences were observed for left ventricular mass index (MD -1.19 g/m², 95% CI -5.63 to 3.24; p=0.597) or systolic blood pressure (MD -8.76 mmHg, 95% CI -20.38 to 2.86; p=0.139).

pico.outcome: Cardiovascular structural and functional parameters (LVEDV, LVEF, PWV, Peak VO2, DBP, SBP, LVMI)

inclusion: Randomised controlled trials involving adults receiving maintenance haemodialysis who underwent structured IDE versus usual care or non-exercise controls and reported cardiac, vascular or cardiorespiratory outcomes

appraisal.bottom_line: Intradialytic exercise significantly improved left ventricular ejection fraction (MD 2.21%, p=0.025), reduced pulse wave velocity (MD -1.36 m/s, p=0.031), and lowered diastolic blood pressure (MD -4.54 mmHg, p=0.003), though it did not significantly affect left ventricular mass index or systolic blood pressure.
appraisal.relevance: Incorporating structured exercise during hemodialysis sessions may offer a practical way to improve cardiovascular function and arterial stiffness in a highly sedentary population.
appraisal.caveat: The findings are limited by low-to-moderate certainty of evidence, substantial heterogeneity for peak VO2 (I²=90.07%) and SBP (I²=73.20%), and high risk of bias in individual contributing trials.

articles.authors: Câmara LC, da Costa Viana DP, de Sousa Monte Alto L, Mattoso SO, Junior NC et al.
articles.title: Effects of nandrolone decanoate on lean body mass and anemia in adults with chronic kidney disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.summary: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 15 RCTs (published 1974-2021, n=312 total across analyzed subsets) evaluating intramuscular nandrolone decanoate in adults with CKD. Nandrolone decanoate was associated with increased lean body mass (4 trials, n=125, MD 2.63 kg, 95% CI 1.60-3.65). Pooled estimates for hemoglobin (6 trials, n=239, MD 0.81 g/dL) and hematocrit (7 trials, n=198, MD 3.12%) also favored nandrolone, but were limited by substantial heterogeneity and very low certainty of evidence.

pico.comparison: Control (not specified, likely placebo or standard care)
pico.outcome: Lean body mass, hemoglobin, hematocrit, quality of life, and safety

inclusion: Randomized controlled trials of intramuscular nandrolone decanoate in adults with CKD

appraisal.bottom_line: Nandrolone decanoate was associated with an increase in lean body mass (MD 2.63 kg, 95% CI 1.60-3.65), but benefits for hemoglobin and hematocrit remain highly uncertain due to substantial heterogeneity and very low certainty of evidence.
appraisal.relevance: While anabolic steroids could theoretically address protein-energy wasting and anemia in CKD, the current evidence is outdated and insufficient to support routine clinical use.
appraisal.caveat: The included trials are largely historical (ranging from 1974 to 2021), have very small sample sizes, lack long-term safety data, and exhibit substantial heterogeneity, rendering the hematologic findings highly uncertain.

articles.authors: Hmida M, Abouzida MA, Bardiaa Y, Abed KE
articles.title: Acute Haemodynamic and Perceptual Responses to Graded Intradialytic Exercise in Patients on Maintenance Haemodialysis: A Randomised Crossover Trial.
articles.summary: A randomized crossover trial in 48 stable maintenance hemodialysis patients comparing graded lower-limb resistance exercise (targeting Borg CR10 ratings of 3, 5, and 7) to a seated control. Graded exercise produced dose-dependent increases in hemodynamic parameters. Compared with control, higher perceived intensity increased systolic blood pressure by 14.9 mmHg (95% CI 12.7-17.0), diastolic blood pressure by 8.4 mmHg (6.8-10.0), mean arterial pressure by 10.6 mmHg (9.2-12.0), and heart rate by 15.5 bpm (12.9-18.1). No serious adverse events occurred.

pico.population: Clinically stable adults receiving maintenance haemodialysis (n=48)
pico.intervention: Graded lower-limb resistance exercise targeting Borg category-ratio 10 ratings of 3, 5, and 7
pico.outcome: Systolic and diastolic blood pressure, mean arterial pressure, heart rate, peripheral oxygen saturation, rating of perceived exertion, acute fatigue, and adverse events

inclusion: Clinically stable adults receiving maintenance haemodialysis

appraisal.bottom_line: Graded intradialytic resistance exercise led to dose-dependent increases in blood pressure (SBP +14.9 mmHg, DBP +8.4 mmHg) and heart rate (+15.5 bpm) without causing serious adverse events or oxygen desaturation below 90%.
appraisal.relevance: This study provides physiological reassurance that graded resistance exercise is acutely tolerated during dialysis, though it transiently increases hemodynamic load.
appraisal.caveat: The trial only assessed acute, single-session physiological and perceptual responses; it does not establish the long-term safety, adherence, or clinical efficacy of sustained high-intensity intradialytic training.

articles.title: Surgical Considerations for Kidney Transplant in Simultaneous Versus Sequential Heart-Kidney Transplant: A Systematic Review.
articles.summary: A systematic review of 35 full-text records examining surgical timing for kidney transplantation in simultaneous heart-kidney transplant (SHKT). SHKT was most supported in dialysis-dependent recipients and those with severe, irreversible renal dysfunction. Kidney delayed graft function (DGF) occurred in 1/4 to 1/3 of SHKT recipients and was associated with worse survival. Sequential kidney-after-heart transplant (SKAHT) was suggested as a reasonable strategy when renal reversibility is uncertain or the post-surgery heart transplant environment is hostile to renal graft perfusion.

pico.population: Adults undergoing or considered for heart-kidney transplantation
pico.intervention: Simultaneous heart-kidney transplant (immediate or staged kidney implantation)
pico.outcome: Kidney delayed graft function (DGF), patient survival, kidney graft survival, primary nonfunction, early kidney graft loss, and renal allograft futility

inclusion: MEDLINE/Embase/Cochrane records from January 1, 2006, through March 21, 2026
Organ Procurement and Transplant Network policy reports
exclusion: Studies outside the specified date range

appraisal.bottom_line: Simultaneous heart-kidney transplant is most supported for dialysis-dependent or severe irreversible renal failure, but sequential kidney-after-heart transplant is a viable alternative when renal reversibility is uncertain or hemodynamic instability threatens early graft perfusion.
appraisal.relevance: Distinguishing simultaneous allocation from simultaneous implantation allows transplant teams to optimize organ stewardship and patient outcomes by delaying kidney implantation in hemodynamically unstable recipients.
appraisal.caveat: This is a qualitative systematic review of largely retrospective, observational data and policy reports, meaning it cannot establish causal superiority of one surgical timing strategy over another, and is subject to selection bias.

articles.authors: Aziz A, Abbas S, Aftab A, Naqvi R
articles.title: Poisons causing acute kidney injury in Indo-Pak region: A meta-analysis.
articles.summary: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 19 studies (12 from India, 7 from Pakistan, n=3,769 total patients) evaluating acute kidney injury caused by exposure to different poisons. Paraphenylene diamine (PPD) poisoning was the sole focus of 10 studies (52.6%). The pooled mortality rate was 20% to 23%, with fixed and random-effect model estimates being 0.23 (95% CI: 0.22-0.25) and 0.20 (95% CI: 0.12-0.28), respectively. High heterogeneity (I² = 90%) and publication bias were observed.

pico.population: Patients with poisoning-induced acute kidney injury in India and Pakistan (n=3,769 across 19 studies)
pico.intervention: Exposure to various poisons (e.g., paraphenylene diamine, paraquat, organophosphate, copper sulphate, methyl alcohol, rodenticides)
pico.outcome: All-group mortality and subgroup mortality for paraphenylene diamine poisoning

inclusion: Studies from India and Pakistan addressing acute kidney injury resulting from exposure to different poisons

appraisal.bottom_line: Poisoning-induced acute kidney injury in the Indo-Pak region—frequently caused by paraphenylene diamine—is associated with a high pooled mortality rate of 20% to 23% (random-effects estimate: 0.20, 95% CI 0.12-0.28).
appraisal.relevance: Understanding the local epidemiology of nephrotoxic poisons is critical for clinicians in South Asia to prompt early recognition, supportive care, and potential extracorporeal therapies.
appraisal.caveat: The analysis is limited by extreme heterogeneity (I² = 90%) and significant publication bias among the included observational studies, which mostly represent single-center retrospective cohorts with varying clinical protocols.
